title: Install and maintain irrigation controllers and climatic sensors

lessons.title: Types of irrigation controllers and installation
lessons.html:
What a controller does

An irrigation controller is the timer and brain of an automatic system. It sends a low-voltage signal (usually 24 V AC) to solenoid valves to open them in sequence for set run times, and may start a pump through a relay.

Types of controllers

TypeDescriptionTypical use
Battery-operated tap or valve timersSingle valve, no mains powerSmall gardens, remote spots
Conventional (multi-wire) controllersOne wire from each station to its valve plus a common wireHomes, small estates
Modular controllersStation modules can be addedGrowing sites
Two-wire (decoder) controllersOne two-wire cable loops past all valves; a decoder at each valve reads its addressGolf courses, sportsfields, large parks
Smart / ET-based controllersAdjust schedules from weather data or on-site sensors; often Wi-Fi or app basedWater-wise landscapes
Central control systemsComputer or cloud manages many field controllersMunicipal parks, large sites

Choosing a location

  • Close to a reliable power supply and as central as possible to the valves.
  • Indoor models in a garage or pump room; outdoor models in a weather-rated, lockable enclosure, out of direct sun if possible.
  • At a comfortable working height, accessible for programming.
  • Away from flood risk and away from where garden sprinklers spray.

Installing

  1. Mount the controller level and secure with suitable fixings.
  2. The 230 V supply must be installed by a qualified electrician, with a dedicated, protected circuit and earth leakage protection, in line with SANS 10142-1 wiring rules.
  3. Bring field wires into the controller through conduit; label each station wire.
  4. Connect the common wire to COM and station wires to their numbered terminals; connect the pump-start or master valve terminal if used.
  5. Program date, time, start times, run times and watering days.
  6. Test each station manually and confirm the right zone opens.

lessons.title: Lightning protection and climatic sensors
lessons.html:
Lightning protection

South Africa's Highveld has one of the highest lightning densities in the world. Long field cables act like antennae: a nearby strike induces surges that can destroy controller boards and decoders.

Protection measures

  • Earthing: the controller must be bonded to an effective earth: earth spikes or earth plates driven into moist soil, connected with heavy copper conductor, with earth resistance tested to the manufacturer's requirement.
  • Surge arrestors: on the mains supply side and on field wiring (station outputs, two-wire paths, sensor inputs).
  • Two-wire systems: fit surge protection and earthing at intervals along the cable, as the manufacturer specifies, and at decoders.
  • Cable routing: bury cables at the correct depth, in conduit where needed, and avoid running them parallel to fences or overhead lines for long distances.
  • Shielded or twisted cable where recommended.

Never work on controllers or cables during a thunderstorm.

Climatic sensors for water conservation

SensorFunction
Rain sensorInterrupts watering when rain has fallen (cork discs or a tipping bucket)
Wind sensorStops sprinklers in high wind to prevent drift and uneven coverage
Freeze sensorStops watering at low temperatures to prevent ice on paths and plant damage
Soil moisture sensorAllows or blocks watering based on root-zone moisture
Weather station / ET sensorSupplies temperature, humidity, solar radiation, wind and rain data so the controller adjusts run times to evapotranspiration
Flow sensorDetects high flow (burst pipe) or low flow (closed valve) and shuts off zones

Installing sensors

  • Rain sensors: mount in open sky, not under trees or eaves and out of sprinkler spray, usually on a fascia or pole.
  • Wind sensors: mount where they read the wind affecting the irrigated area.
  • Soil moisture sensors: bury in the root zone of a representative zone, in full contact with undisturbed soil, away from drip emitters and edges.
  • Wire sensors to the controller's sensor terminals (or in series with the common wire for older controllers), and enable the sensor input in programming.
  • Test each sensor: wet the rain sensor and confirm watering is suspended.

lessons.title: Maintaining controllers and documentation
lessons.html:
Routine maintenance

TaskFrequency (typical)
Check date, time and programme are correct, especially after power cuts and load sheddingMonthly and after outages
Replace the backup batteryAs manufacturer recommends, or yearly
Adjust run times for the season (or check seasonal adjust %)Each season
Test each station manually; watch zones for faultsMonthly
Clean rain sensor, check cork discs or bucket move freelyEach season
Check enclosure: seals, insects, rodents, moistureQuarterly
Check earth connections and surge arrestors, especially after stormsAfter storms and yearly
Update firmware on smart controllersAs released

Fault finding

  • One station will not open: measure output voltage at the terminal with a multimeter; if present, test the solenoid resistance and the field wire for breaks.
  • Fuse or circuit breaker trips when a station runs: short circuit in the wire or a failed solenoid.
  • No stations work: check power, transformer, common wire, and whether a sensor is holding the system off.
  • Watering at wrong times: overlapping programmes, wrong clock, or extra start times.
  • Controller dead after a storm: surge damage; check earthing and arrestors before replacing the board.

Switch off the mains supply before opening the controller's high-voltage compartment, and leave mains faults to an electrician.

Documentation

  • As-built plan: controller location, station numbers, valve locations, wire routes and colours.
  • Station chart: inside the controller door showing each station's area and run time.
  • Programme record: start times, run times, watering days, sensor settings.
  • Earth test results and surge device details.
  • Maintenance log: date, work done, faults, parts replaced.
  • Manuals and warranty information handed to the client.

Key points

  • Choose the controller type to suit the site size and control needs.
  • Mains supply is installed by a qualified electrician; field wiring is low voltage.
  • Earth controllers well and fit surge arrestors in lightning-prone areas.
  • Use rain, wind, freeze, soil moisture and ET sensors to save water.
  • Check programmes after power cuts and keep full records.

quiz.question: Where should a rain sensor be mounted?

options.text: In open sky, out of sprinkler spray and not under trees

quiz.question: What does a flow sensor help detect?

options.text: A burst pipe or closed valve

quiz.question: A fuse trips every time station 4 runs. What is the likely cause?

options.text: A short circuit in the wire or a failed solenoid
